subtype: Approach: giving up when the goal seems too far [Pitfall]
passage: After two weeks of dropping coins in the jar, Chaitanya looked at the total and sighed. Only Rs 90. The remote-control car cost Rs 600. "That will take forever," he told Avni at recess. "Then why not buy something else?" Avni said, shrugging. That evening Chaitanya broke the jar and bought a cheap plastic car from the corner stall. It looked good for a day. On the third day, one wheel fell off and the steering stopped working. He sat with the broken toy in his hands, the jar empty, the money gone, and the real car further away than ever.

qa.q: How much money did Chaitanya have after two weeks?
qa.a: Chaitanya had Rs 90 after two weeks.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he decided to break the jar?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt discouraged and impatient, because the goal seemed too far away and he wanted something now. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Chaitanya use, and why?
qa.a: Chaitanya could set a smaller first target and mark each step, because shorter goals feel reachable. Asking a parent for a way to earn extra could also help.

qa.q: How might Avni see the choice to buy the cheap car?
qa.a: Avni suggested buying something else and shrugged, so Avni may not have realised how much the savings and the goal mattered to Chaitanya.

grounding: After two weeks a boy decides that 600 rupees will take too long, spends the savings on a cheap toy that breaks and ends up with less than planned.

subtype: Approach: giving up when the goal seems too far [Pitfall]
passage:
"Didi, I've saved for two weeks and I've only got a hundred rupees."
"And the drone is six hundred?"
"Six hundred! It'll take forever." Arnab shook the tin. "The shop near the bus stop has a plastic helicopter for eighty. It lights up."
"You said you wanted the drone."
"I want something now."
Two days later:
"Didi... the propeller fell off."
Ishita looked at the helicopter on the floor, its light flickering. "Already?"
"And now the light's stopped." Arnab turned the tin upside down. Twenty rupees fell out. "I've got less than when I started."
"Want to start again?"
He looked at the twenty rupees for a long time.

qa.q: How much did the plastic helicopter cost?
How did Arnab feel when the tin showed twenty rupees?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and regretful, with less than when he started and a broken toy.

qa.q: What could have helped Arnab when the goal felt too far?
qa.a: A smaller first target, or counting the weeks left with a parent; buying something now emptied the tin for a toy that broke.

qa.q: How does Ishita seem to see Arnab's choice?
qa.a: Ishita reminded him he wanted the drone and, after it broke, gently asks if he wants to start again, so she seems patient and kind.

grounding: Shows a boy who, after two weeks, feels six hundred rupees will take forever, spends his savings on a cheap toy that breaks, and ends up with less.

subtype: Approach: giving up when the goal seems too far [Pitfall]
passage: In Class 4 I was saving for a Rs 600 football, the real leather kind. After two weeks I had Rs 120, and I remember thinking: at this speed, I'll be in Class 5 before I get it. It felt like forever. So one evening, when Samir and I passed the fair, I spent all of it on a plastic car with flashing wheels. It was great for exactly three days. Then one wheel snapped, and the flashing stopped. I remember holding it and feeling stupid. I'd had Rs 120 and a plan; now I had a broken car and nothing in my tin. Samir said, 'Bhupen, you should've waited.' He was right.

qa.q: How much had Bhupen saved after two weeks?
How did Bhupen feel holding the broken car?
qa.a: Bhupen felt stupid and regretful, having swapped a plan and Rs 120 for a broken toy.

qa.q: What could Bhupen have tried when Rs 600 felt so far away?
qa.a: A smaller first target, like Rs 200, or asking a parent to help plan the weeks, instead of spending everything at the fair.

qa.q: How does Samir see what happened?
qa.a: Samir thinks Bhupen should have waited, and says so plainly.

grounding: Illustrates a boy giving up on a Rs 600 goal after two weeks, spending his savings on a cheap toy that breaks within days, and ending up with less.
